description:
We’re Ajitesh and Praney Bankula, two brothers who like building things together. Ajitesh is pursuing a BS in Computer Science at RPI and an MS in Computer Science at UIUC. Praney is pursuing a bachelor’s in Computer Engineering at Purdue.

We built Umbra-X to explore a question we kept coming back to: what would it take to land and operate on the Moon? We like turning research and real data into tools people can try for themselves.
summary:
At the Moon’s south pole, the Sun stays near the horizon. Crater rims can block sunlight and hide Earth for days, affecting a lander’s power supply and communication opportunities. Choosing a landing pad therefore means choosing when to land—and how to handle a delay.

Umbra-X is an interactive 3D tool for comparing lunar landing plans and finding alternatives. Explore 2,883 candidate pads across Shackleton Ridge, Malapert Massif, and Mons Mouton. Change the pad, landing date, or mast height, then scrub a timeline to inspect sunlight, shadows, and Earth visibility. Set darkness, slope, and power constraints to identify where a plan fails.

The model combines NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL DE440 Sun/Earth positions with 360° terrain horizons, finite solar-disk and eclipse geometry, and geometric visibility to three NASA Deep Space Network stations. Solar-array and battery estimates connect those conditions to equipment mass.

When a plan exceeds the chosen limits, Recover Pads uses a Rust/WebAssembly solver to search alternative pads, heights, and dates across seven objectives, exposing their trade-offs. Umbra Agent explains results with cited sources. Documented assumptions distinguish modeled geometry from operational communications and landing safety.

Built for early mission screening, research, and teaching, Umbra-X helps users understand which choices matter and why.

App: https://umbra-x.mbra.workers.dev/?intro=1

details:
We came to Umbra-X with one simple question: What would it take to land and operate at a particular spot on the Moon?

At the lunar south pole, the answer can change from one ridge to the next. The Sun stays so low that terrain far beyond the landing pad can put a lander in shadow. The same landscape shapes when the lander can see Earth. A flatter site might spend longer in darkness. A taller mast might clear a ridge sooner. Once you put a landing date, a battery budget, and a limit on how long you can lose sight of Earth into the same problem, the choice gets a lot more interesting.

We built Umbra-X so you can work through those decisions yourself. You can start in orbit, come down to the surface, and follow the effect of a single ridge all the way to the amount of battery mass a lander might need.

Explore the terrain and compare two plans

Umbra-X includes 2,883 candidate pads across Shackleton Ridge, Malapert Massif, and Mons Mouton. You can view the terrain from orbit, look toward the Sun or Earth from a pad, switch to a 360° sky view, or read the skyline as a 2D horizon profile. Map overlays show coarse slope, illumination, Earth visibility, and mapped permanently shadowed regions. You can also enter custom coordinates or compare a polar site with a reference location such as Apollo 11. Where we lack regional terrain coverage, the app makes that clear.

The planner puts a baseline and an alternative side by side. What happens if you move to the next pad? Would a 20 m mast change the view compared with a 1.5 m mast? Is it worth looking in another region altogether? Scrubbing the timeline lets you see when the Sun or Earth passes behind the terrain. You can line up the two scenarios by time since landing or by calendar date, depending on what you want to compare.

What one comparison taught us

In one study, we kept the pad and mast height fixed at Shackleton Ridge and moved the landing by 48 hours. Over the 15-day study window, the longest stretch with Earth hidden behind terrain dropped from 103.7 to 55.7 hours, bringing it under the study’s 72-hour limit. The longest stretch of low light stayed at 52.3 hours, above the 48-hour limit, and the pad’s modeled 5.60° slope still exceeded the 5° limit. A two-day delay helped with Earth visibility. We still had to do something about the darkness and slope.

That’s where Recover Pads comes in. You can set how far to look and how much the schedule can change, then compare alternatives on seven measures: darkness, Earth obstruction, slope, battery mass, relocation distance, schedule change, and how well each option holds up under the checks we ran. The closest pad and the pad with the lowest battery requirement may be different places. The search keeps those trade-offs visible so you can decide which one matters more. If no tested option passes, Umbra-X can show near misses and identify the limits they exceed.

The Power & Cost panel lets you take a promising site one step further. You can change the mission’s electrical load, solar array assumptions, and mass budget. The model follows the battery as it charges in sunlight and supplies the load when generation drops. Two pads can get similar total hours of sunlight and still need different batteries if one has a single long stretch of shadow. You can also enter a delivery price per kilogram to see what the difference in equipment mass could cost.

The research behind the math

We started by looking at how researchers turn lunar elevation data into a prediction about sunlight. Mazarico and colleagues showed how to trace the height of the horizon in different directions using NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter, or LOLA. That gave us the basis for one of the main calculations in Umbra-X. From each pad, we follow the terrain in 360 directions and calculate the angle from the observer to each sampled point, accounting for the Moon’s curvature. The highest angle along each direction becomes part of the skyline. A distant ridge can set that angle even when the ground around the pad looks flat. Mazarico et al., lunar polar illumination study

Barker and colleagues studied how errors in LOLA elevations can carry through to the calculated horizon and change the predicted lighting. That mattered to us because a small difference in the skyline can change the answer when the Sun is grazing it. We use 20 m LOLA data near the pad and 80 m data farther out, then use the published elevation uncertainty to test how sensitive a result is. James Fincannon’s NASA power analysis helped us frame the battery question around the timing and duration of shadow. We used that idea to connect our own illumination timeline to an energy balance. Barker et al., elevation uncertainty and illumination · Fincannon, Lunar Polar Illumination for Power Analysis

Every five minutes, the model places the Sun and Earth in the observer’s local sky using JPL DE440 and lunar orientation kernels. The Sun has a visible disk, so a ridge can cover part of it before covering all of it. The model accounts for that partial exposure and for eclipses. We cross-checked our position calculations against JPL Horizons and our slope estimates against NASA’s published LOLA slope product. For Earth visibility, we added a geometric check involving Deep Space Network stations at Goldstone, Madrid, and Canberra. JPL DE440 documentation · JPL Horizons · NASA LOLA data products · DSN Coverage and Geometry

How we built it and what we want people to take from it

We built the interface in TypeScript and React, rendered the terrain with Three.js and React Three Fiber, and used Python to process the terrain rasters and prepare the horizon and ephemeris data. Rust compiled to WebAssembly supports the recovery search, and browser workers run calculations while you interact with the views. Umbra Agent helps explain the results with cited research, and you can export event and analysis data to check the numbers yourself.

We built Umbra-X for early mission screening, research, and teaching. We also wanted the limits to be visible at the point where someone is making a decision. A 20 m elevation grid can flag a steep area. Choosing where to put a lander’s feet would require finer terrain data. A clear line of sight tells you when communication is geometrically possible. Planning actual contact would also require radio and antenna details and a station schedule.

The part we most wanted to get right was the connection between what you see and what you decide. You can watch a ridge cover the Sun, find that moment in the timeline, and see how it changes the battery estimate. If that makes you reconsider the pad, you can try another and see exactly what you gain and what you give up.
